extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics majors and instructors (introductory proofs/discrete mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style guide to learning and writing mathematical proofs for undergraduate mathematics majors; covers foundations (sets, logic, counting), main proof techniques (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction), and topics on relations, functions, and cardinality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sets (basic definitions and notation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is a collection of things; elements, equality of sets, notation (brace listing and set-builder), special sets (N, Z, Q, R), empty set, cardinality |A|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use braces to list elements, set-builder notation X = {expression : rule}, be careful distinguishing absolute value bars vs cardinality bars, careful writing of the empty set (0 = {} not {0}). Examples and exercises illustrate listing elements, intervals, and special sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian Product and Ordered Pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of ordered pair (x,y) and Cartesian product A x B = {(a,b): a∈A, b∈B}; Cartesian powers A^n and products of multiple sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize A x B as a rectangular array; note difference between IR x (N x Z) and IR x N x Z (parentheses matter); if A and B finite then |A x B| = |A|·|B|. Extend to triples, n-tuples, and Cartesian powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsets and Power Sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition A ⊆ B (every element of A is in B), facts such as ∅ ⊆ B for any B, and the power set P(A) = {X : X ⊆ A}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If |A| = n finite then |P(A)| = 2^n. Use tree/branching diagrams to list subsets; mind elements that are themselves sets (distinction between elements and subsets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements and Logical Connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand what a statement is and the basic logical connectives: and, or, not; truth values and truth tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate English assertions to symbolic logic; use truth tables to test compound statements and logical equivalence; practice with examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional and Biconditional Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditional (If P then Q) and biconditional (P iff Q) statements, their meanings and roles in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters focused on techniques for proving conditional statements (direct, contrapositive, contradiction). For iff proofs, prove both directions separately (P→Q and Q→P).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth Tables and Logical Equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use truth tables to establish logical equivalence between statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply DeMorgan's laws and equivalences systematically when simplifying or transforming logical statements; use equivalence when rewriting goals in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers and Negation of Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal and existential quantifiers (∀, ∃), how to interpret and negate quantified statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay careful attention to scope of quantifiers when translating informal English to symbolic logic and when forming negations (switch quantifiers and negate the predicate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating English to Symbolic Logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting everyday mathematical English statements into precise symbolic logical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is emphasized to avoid ambiguity; problems and examples train students to identify predicates, quantifiers, and logical structure before proving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules and techniques for deducing conclusions from premises (inference rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established inference patterns to move from assumptions to conclusions within a proof; exercises develop skill in chaining implications and using earlier results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting Principles (combinatorial reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic counting techniques: counting lists, factorials, counting subsets, Pascal's Triangle and the Binomial Theorem, inclusion–exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiplication/addition principles, factorials, and inclusion–exclusion to count combinatorial structures; many examples and exercises provided for practice and application in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Technique for proving conditional statements by assuming the hypothesis and deducing the conclusion using definitions and earlier results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters include 'Theorems', 'Definitions', 'Direct Proof', and 'Using Cases' — start from definitions and known facts, proceed with straightforward logical deduction; examples show structure and style of direct proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Cases (proof by cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof technique that splits the proof into a finite number of cases that together cover all possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify exhaustive, mutually exclusive cases; prove the desired conclusion in each case; treat similar cases efficiently (see 'Treating Similar Cases').

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating Similar Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When cases in a proof are similar in argument, avoid redundant repetition by indicating the common reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group analogous cases and state once why the same argument applies to each, to keep proofs concise and readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove 'If P then Q' by proving its contrapositive 'If not Q then not P'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when direct implication is hard to establish; examples include congruence of integers and typical number-theory proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by Contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired statement and derive a contradiction, thereby concluding the original statement is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapters detail 'Proving Statements with Contradiction', 'Proving Conditional Statements by Contradiction', and discuss combining techniques; use when negation leads to a clear impossibility or conflict with known facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining Proof Techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective proofs often combine multiple techniques (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, induction) as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible: if one approach stalls, try another or combine approaches; examples show transitions and hybrid proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Writing (exposition and style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on writing clear mathematical proofs and exposition (section noted as 'Mathematical Writing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize clarity, use of definitions, logical order, proper notation, and concise presentation; the text includes exercises and 'Some Words of Advice' to improve exposition and avoid common stylistic mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: If-and-Only-If Proofs (biconditional proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving biconditional statements by demonstrating both directions separately (P⇒Q and Q⇒P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether a single argument can be adapted for both directions or if distinct methods are required for each implication; exercises provide practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent Statements and Reformulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and use equivalent formulations of a statement to simplify proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform a target statement into an equivalent but more tractable form (logical equivalence, algebraic manipulations, set-theoretic identities) before proving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and Uniqueness Proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove that an object exists (existence) and/or that it is the only such object (uniqueness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies include constructive proofs (exhibit an example) and non-constructive proofs (show existence indirectly); for uniqueness, assume two such objects and show they must be equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive vs Non-Constructive Proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between proofs that explicitly construct an example and proofs that show existence without providing a construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses the distinction and when each style is appropriate; constructive proofs are often more informative, but non-constructive arguments are acceptable when construction is difficult or unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs Involving Sets (how to prove subset and equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific methods for set proofs: how to show A ⊆ B, how to show A = B (usually by proving A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use element-chasing: take arbitrary x∈A and show x∈B for subset proofs; for equality prove both inclusions; examples (including perfect numbers) illustrate techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples and Disproofs
rubrics_metrics.description: To disprove a universal statement, provide a counterexample; techniques for disproving existence statements (including disproof by contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 9 emphasizes constructing counterexamples and shows methods for disproving existence claims and how contradiction can serve to disprove statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical Induction (including strong and smallest counterexample)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is a method for proving statements about integers: base case and inductive step; variations include strong induction and proof by smallest counterexample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 10 covers ordinary induction, strong induction (assume statement holds for all ≤k to prove k+1), and proof by smallest counterexample; worked examples include Fibonacci numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations: properties and equivalence relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and properties of relations (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), equivalence relations, equivalence classes, and partitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove properties by verifying definitions for arbitrary elements; use equivalence classes to partition sets and illustrate with modular arithmetic examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions: definitions and key properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of function, domain, codomain, range; injective (one-to-one), surjective (onto), bijection; composition and inverse functions; image and preimage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide proofs of injectivity/surjectivity by direct arguments or constructive mappings; use composition and inverse definitions to manipulate and prove identities about functions; exercises include pigeonhole principle applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality and Comparing Sizes of Sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Cardinality notions: finite, countably infinite, uncountable; comparing cardinalities, bijections, Cantor-Bernstein-Schroeder theorem, and examples showing equalities |R|=|(0,1)| and |P(N)|>|R|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit bijections, injections, and surjections to compare sizes; apply Cantor's diagonal argument and Cantor-Bernstein-Schroeder where appropriate; many illustrative exercises and proofs.
